messages.subject: Building nimble model with large datasets (n>1 million)
parts:
Hello, 

I have a question about nimble's scalability for large n problems. Below is code for a very simple toy example of a simple logistic regression where n=1e+06. Ultimately, I'd like to obtain posterior samples from the posterior distribution p(b1,b2|z). Note that there are no large matrix operations (i.e., inverses, determinants) nor are we dealing with high-dimensional set of model parameters. 

However, I am unable to even build an MCMC sampler due to the large size of the dataset. The process is shut down during the nimbleFunction() evaluation. For smaller datasets (n=3e+05), the bulk of the walltime is attributed to building the nimble model (highlighted below).  Once the model is built, everything else proceeds very smoothly. 

Do you have any tips for using nimble with very large datasets? Is there a way to build the nimble models faster using nimbleFunction()?

Thank you so much. 

Ben

 

#Toy Example

# Generate Binary Data 
n=1000000
beta<-c(1,1)
XMat<-cbind(runif(n,-1,1),runif(n,-1,1))
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize
consts   <- list(n=n)
data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat)
inits    <- list(beta1=0,beta2=0)

# Model String
model_binary_string_conj <- nimbleCode({
  # Data Model
  for(i in 1:n){
    prob[i] <- exp(XB[i])/(1+exp(XB[i]))
    Z[i] ~ dbern(prob[i])
  }
  XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]
  
  # Parameter Model
  beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
  beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})


# Build Model
Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string_conj, data = data,  
                    constants=consts, inits = inits)
cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)
RmodelConf$printSamplers()
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta1", "beta2"))
bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC)

# Run sampler
niter=1000
cMCMC$run(niter)
samples_extended <- as.matrix(cMCMC$mvSamples)

Hi Ben, 

here a couple of tips. A first tip would be to use the argument calculate = FALSE when using the nimbleModel() function, which will build the nimble models faster. By default, calculate is set to TRUE, meaning that nimble calculates all deterministic nodes and logProbability values when creating the model, and with large models this can eat up a good amount of time and memory.

Second, it may be helpful in this case to write Z and prob in a vectorized form; this should help in that the resulting model would have less nodes to handle (i.e. two vector nodes instead of 2xn scalar nodes).  To do so, you would need a user-defined distribution for the vectorized version of the Bernoulli variable, that takes a vector of probabilities and returns the total log-probability.  If you are not familiar with user-defined distributions, they are covered in Chapter 12.2 of the User Manual, plus there are a couple of examples using them in our examples page on the website ("Writing a new distribution" and the "stochastic volatility" ones). And of course, feel free to ask for clarifications here!

Anyway, I've modified your example including these two tips and been able to try it out on my laptop. Let me know how it works for you, or if something is unclear. 

Best, 

Sally


###############################
# Toy Example
library(nimble)

# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000
beta<-c(1,1)
XMat<-cbind(runif(n,-1,1),runif(n,-1,1))
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize
consts   <- list(n=n)
data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat)
inits    <- list(beta1=0,beta2=0)

# SP: user defined distribution
# for a vector of bernoulli variables

dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),
                 log  = integer(0, default = 1)) {

    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

# Model String

model_binary_string_conj <- nimbleCode({
    # Data Model

# SP: vectorized version using a user defined distribution
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1 + exp(XB[1:n]))
    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])

XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]

    # Parameter Model
    beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
    beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})

Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string_conj,
                    data = data,
                    constants=consts,

inits = inits,
                    calculate = FALSE) ## this should help to reduce memory & time

cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)
RmodelConf$printSamplers()
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta1", "beta2"))
bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC, project = Rmodel)

# Run sampler
niter=1000
cMCMC$run(niter)
gsamples_extended <- as.matrix(cMCMC$mvSamples)

Hi Ben, 

here a couple of tips. A first tip would be to use the argument calculate = FALSE when using the nimbleModel() function, which will build the nimble models faster. By default, calculate is set to TRUE, meaning that nimble calculates all deterministic nodes and logProbability values when creating the model, and with large models this can eat up a good amount of time and memory.

Second, it may be helpful in this case to write Z and prob in a vectorized form; this should help in that the resulting model would have less nodes to handle (i.e. two vector nodes instead of 2xn scalar nodes).  To do so, you would need a user-defined distribution for the vectorized version of the Bernoulli variable, that takes a vector of probabilities and returns the total log-probability.  If you are not familiar with user-defined distributions, they are covered in Chapter 12.2 of the User Manual, plus there are a couple of examples using them in our examples page on the website ("Writing a new distribution" and the "stochastic volatility" ones). And of course, feel free to ask for clarifications here!

Anyway, I've modified your example including these two tips and been able to try it out on my laptop. Let me know how it works for you, or if something is unclear. 

Best, 

Sally

# Toy Example
library(nimble)

# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000
beta<-c(1,1)
XMat<-cbind(runif(n,-1,1),runif(n,-1,1))
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize
consts   <- list(n=n)
data     <- list(Z=z,X=XMat)
inits    <- list(beta1=0,beta2=0)

# SP: user defined distribution
# for a vector of bernoulli variables

dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),
                 log  = integer(0, default = 1)) {

    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

# Model String

model_binary_string_conj <- nimbleCode({
    # Data Model
   
    # SP: vectorized version using a user defined distribution
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1 + exp(XB[1:n]))
    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])



XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]

    # Parameter Model
    beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
    beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})

cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC, project = Rmodel)

Hi Ben,

There are several reasons nimble encounters scaling issues.  For any model variable, nimble needs to allow for complete generality of how nodes may be declared in arbitrary ways for indexed subsets of a variable and how arbitrary subsets of it (not necessarily corresponding to declared nodes) may be used as arguments for other declarations.  nimble then needs to make a graph from all that generality.  This leads to a fair bit of bookkeeping.  There are some ways to improve this that we have on our agenda, and one of them is currently lined up in a pull request on github.  Some of the issues that arise have to do with R scaling issues for the steps we implement in R.  There are deeper ways to envision better scaling, but they will be longer term.

Back to your needs: Here is a way to work around some of nimble's scaling issues.  You can use nimbleRcall to keep large constant objects entirely out of the model.  In the example below, I have kept X and pCov out of the model.  In effect, nimble is still managing the model graph and using its MCMC system, but some of the big calculations are thrown back to R.  There will be some overhead from going back to R, but maybe those costs won't be too bad compared to the cost of the large calculations.  Of course, I don't know if you want to expand the model to have X and/or pCov be non-constant, but if so you can build on the basic scheme shown below.  It would also be possible to have the large objects like X and pCov be in C++ objects used by C++ functions via nimbleExternalCall, but that would take some direct C++ coding.

With the code below, everything builds reasonably quickly.

library(nimble)

#Toy Example
# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000 ; k=200
#n <- 100000; k <- 100 # smaller case Perry used for prototyping

beta<-rep(1,k)
XMat<-matrix(rnorm(n*k),nrow=n,ncol=k)
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize

keepInR <- list(X=XMat, pCov=100*diag(k))
consts   <- list(n=n,k=k)
data     <- list(Z=z, mn=rep(0,k))

inits    <- list(beta=rep(0,k))

# for a vector of bernoulli variables
dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),
log  = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero

returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

## Use R's lexical scoping to create R functions to be called
## via nimbleRcall that will find large objects like
## X and pCov in their enclosing environment.
makeRfuns <- function(keepInR) {
  X <- keepInR$X
  pCov <- keepInR$pCov
  chol_pCov <- chol(pCov)
  RcalculateXB <- function(beta) {
    as.numeric(X %*% beta)
  }
  dRdmnorm <- function(x, mean, log) {
    nimble::dmnorm_chol(x, mean, cholesky = chol_pCov, prec_param = FALSE, log = log)
  }
  list(RcalculateXB = RcalculateXB, dRdmnorm = dRdmnorm)
}

## Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
Rfuns <- makeRfuns(keepInR)
RcalculateXB_internal <- Rfuns$RcalculateXB ## I think these need to be in .GlobalEnv
dRdmnorm_internal <- Rfuns$dRdmnorm

## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R functions.
RcalculateXB <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(1)) {}, returnType = double(1), Rfun = 'RcalculateXB_internal')
dRdmnorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(1), mean = double(1), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {}, returnType = double(), Rfun = 'dRdmnorm_internal')

## Write the model using the nimbleRcalls.  Note that X and pCov do not appear in the model.

# Model String
model_binary_string <- nimbleCode({
  # Data Model
    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1+exp(XB[1:n]))

XB[1:n] <- RcalculateXB(beta[1:k])
 
  # Parameter Model
  beta[1:k] ~ dRdmnorm(mean = mn[1:k])

})


# Build Model
Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string, data = data,  
                    constants=consts, inits = inits,calculate = FALSE)

system.time(cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel))
system.time(RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)) ## could use useConjugacy=FALSE
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta"))
system.time(bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf))
system.time(cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC))
system.time(cMCMC$run(10))

Hi Perry, 

Thank you very much for looking into this for me and explaining why we experience scaling issues, particularly when interfacing with R. Hi Ben,

There are several reasons nimble encounters scaling issues.  For any model variable, nimble needs to allow for complete generality of how nodes may be declared in arbitrary ways for indexed subsets of a variable and how arbitrary subsets of it (not necessarily corresponding to declared nodes) may be used as arguments for other declarations.  nimble then needs to make a graph from all that generality.  This leads to a fair bit of bookkeeping.  There are some ways to improve this that we have on our agenda, and one of them is currently lined up in a pull request on github.  Some of the issues that arise have to do with R scaling issues for the steps we implement in R.  There are deeper ways to envision better scaling, but they will be longer term.

Back to your needs: Here is a way to work around some of nimble's scaling issues.  You can use nimbleRcall to keep large constant objects entirely out of the model.  In the example below, I have kept X and pCov out of the model.  In effect, nimble is still managing the model graph and using its MCMC system, but some of the big calculations are thrown back to R.  There will be some overhead from going back to R, but maybe those costs won't be too bad compared to the cost of the large calculations.  Of course, I don't know if you want to expand the model to have X and/or pCov be non-constant, but if so you can build on the basic scheme shown below.  It would also be possible to have the large objects like X and pCov be in C++ objects used by C++ functions via nimbleExternalCall, but that would take some direct C++ coding.

With the code below, everything builds reasonably quickly.

library(nimble)


#Toy Example
# Generate Binary Data
n=1000000 ; k=200
#n <- 100000; k <- 100 # smaller case Perry used for prototyping

beta<-rep(1,k)
XMat<-matrix(rnorm(n*k),nrow=n,ncol=k)
linPred<-as.numeric(XMat%*%beta)
prob<-exp(linPred)/(1+exp(linPred))
z<-sapply(prob,rbinom,n=1,size=1)

# Initialize
keepInR <- list(X=XMat, pCov=100*diag(k))
consts   <- list(n=n,k=k)
data     <- list(Z=z, mn=rep(0,k))

inits    <- list(beta=rep(0,k))

# for a vector of bernoulli variables
dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x    = double(1),
                 prob = double(1),
                 log  = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero

   
    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
  }
)

## Use R's lexical scoping to create R functions to be called
## via nimbleRcall that will find large objects like
## X and pCov in their enclosing environment.
makeRfuns <- function(keepInR) {
  X <- keepInR$X
  pCov <- keepInR$pCov
  chol_pCov <- chol(pCov)
  RcalculateXB <- function(beta) {
    as.numeric(X %*% beta)
  }
  dRdmnorm <- function(x, mean, log) {
    nimble::dmnorm_chol(x, mean, cholesky = chol_pCov, prec_param = FALSE, log = log)
  }
  list(RcalculateXB = RcalculateXB, dRdmnorm = dRdmnorm)
}

## Create the functions and put them in .GlobalEnv
Rfuns <- makeRfuns(keepInR)
RcalculateXB_internal <- Rfuns$RcalculateXB ## I think these need to be in .GlobalEnv
dRdmnorm_internal <- Rfuns$dRdmnorm

## Define the nimbleRcall nimbleFunctions to call the R functions.
RcalculateXB <- nimbleRcall(function(beta = double(1)) {}, returnType = double(1), Rfun = 'RcalculateXB_internal')
dRdmnorm <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(1), mean = double(1), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {}, returnType = double(), Rfun = 'dRdmnorm_internal')

## Write the model using the nimbleRcalls.  Note that X and pCov do not appear in the model.

# Model String
model_binary_string <- nimbleCode({
  # Data Model
    Z[1:n] ~ dBernoulliVector(prob[1:n])
    prob[1:n] <- exp(XB[1:n])/(1+exp(XB[1:n]))
    XB[1:n] <- RcalculateXB(beta[1:k])
 
  # Parameter Model
  beta[1:k] ~ dRdmnorm(mean = mn[1:k])

})


# Build Model
Rmodel<-nimbleModel(code=model_binary_string, data = data,  
                    constants=consts, inits = inits,calculate = FALSE)
system.time(cRmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel))
system.time(RmodelConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE, useConjugacy = TRUE)) ## could use useConjugacy=FALSE
RmodelConf$addMonitors(c("beta"))
system.time(bMCMC <- buildMCMC(RmodelConf))
system.time(cMCMC <- compileNimble(bMCMC))
system.time(cMCMC$run(10))
